title: Relations and Functions
tagline: Ordered pairs and Cartesian products, the three properties that classify a relation, and the domain, range and graphs of functions.

overview.intro: A relation links elements of one set to elements of another, and a function is a relation with discipline: one image for every input. This chapter starts at the ordered pair and builds the Cartesian product as its stage, then reads relations as subsets of that stage and tests them for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. The second half turns to functions — the vertical line test, one-one and onto classification, even and odd symmetry — because every later chapter, from trigonometry to derivatives, assumes fluency with domain, range and the shape of a graph.

facts.label: Ordered pair
facts.value: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d; order is the whole content of the pair.

facts.label: Cartesian product
facts.value: A × B holds n(A) × n(B) ordered pairs, and A × B ≠ B × A unless A = B.

facts.label: Function test
facts.value: A relation is a function only when every domain element has exactly one image.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Domain, range and classification of relations and functions are steady short-question topics every year.

learningOutcomes: Form ordered pairs and Cartesian products and count and list their elements.
Read a relation as a subset of A × B and state its domain, range, codomain and inverse.
Test a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity and classify it as an equivalence relation or not.
Decide whether a relation is a function and distinguish one-one, onto, many-one and into functions.
Find the domain and range of a function from its rule and decide from its graph whether it is a function, even or odd.

learn.title: Ordered pairs and the Cartesian product

blocks.text: An ordered pair (a, b) is a pair in which position carries meaning: (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different objects, and equality of pairs demands equality in both slots, so (a, b) = (c, d) precisely when a = c and b = d. The Cartesian product A × B is the set of all ordered pairs with first component in A and second in B, written A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. Its size multiplies: three elements against four gives twelve pairs. The product is neither commutative nor associative in general, but it does distribute across union and intersection — A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C) — and it annihilates emptiness, since A × ∅ and ∅ × B are both empty. If any pair of the products equals the other’s first coordinate, careful bookkeeping with these rules keeps a messy expression honest.

items: (a, b) = (c, d) iff a = c and b = d; (a, b) ≠ (b, a) unless a = b.
n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B), and the listing runs through A for each element of B or the reverse.
A × B ≠ B × A in general, but (A × B) × C and A × (B × C) both hold mnk ordered pairs.
A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C), and the same distributive law holds for intersection.
If A × B = A × C with A non-empty, then B = C; if either factor is empty the product is empty.

items.note: Six pairs = 3 × 2, listed by holding the first component fixed and running through the second.
Both coordinates must match; swapping them breaks the equality.

learn.title: Relations as subsets: domain, range and inverse

blocks.text: A relation from A to B is simply any subset of the Cartesian product A × B, so a relation is defined by which pairs it admits and nothing else. The domain collects the first components of those pairs, the range collects the second components actually used, and the codomain is the whole target set B. The inverse relation R⁻¹ reverses every pair, which swaps the domain of R with the range of R⁻¹. These four objects — R, its domain, its range and its inverse — answer most short questions in this chapter, and they are read directly off a mapping diagram: arrows leave the domain and land in the range, and reversing the arrows draws the inverse.

items: A relation R from A to B is a subset of A × B; the universal relation is A × B itself, the empty relation is ∅.
Domain of R = {first components of the pairs in R}; range = {second components actually used}.
Inverse R⁻¹ = {(b, a) : (a, b) ∈ R}; the domain of R⁻¹ is the range of R.
R is onto B when its range equals B; otherwise the relation does not reach all of the codomain.
A mapping diagram shows the relation: one arrow leaving an element of A means one ordered pair.

items.note: Domain = {1, 2, 3}, range = {2, 3}; the element 4 of the codomain is never used.

items.text: R⁻¹ of the same relation is {(2, 1), (3, 2), (2, 3)}
items.note: Every pair reverses, so the new domain {2, 3} is the old range.

items.meaning: Any subset of A × B, associating some elements of A with some of B.
Set of first components of the pairs of a relation.
Set of second components actually appearing in the pairs.
The whole target set B into which the relation maps.

blocks.text: Three properties classify every relation the syllabus names. A relation is reflexive when every element is related to itself, so (a, a) must belong to R for each a in A; it is symmetric when relating a to b always brings b back to a; and it is transitive when relating a to b and b to c forces a to c. A relation satisfying all three at once is an equivalence relation, and equivalence relations are exactly the ones that sort a set into clean, non-overlapping classes — equality of numbers, equality of triangles by shape, same remainder on division by three. The three properties are tested separately, because a relation may hold any combination of them: a relation can be perfectly symmetric yet fail transitivity the moment one return pair lacks its closure.

items: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A — one missing self-pair destroys it.
Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R implies (b, a) ∈ R for all a, b.
Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R imply (a, c) ∈ R.
Equivalence relation = reflexive + symmetric + transitive, all three together.
The empty relation on a non-empty set is not reflexive; the universal relation always is.

items.note: Reflexive (all three self-pairs present), symmetric (1 and 2 point both ways) and transitive (the products close on existing pairs), so it is an equivalence relation.
Symmetric and reflexive, but (1, 2) and (2, 3) hold while (1, 3) is missing, so S is not transitive.

learn.title: Functions: one-one, onto, even and odd

blocks.text: A function from A to B is a relation in which every element of A has exactly one image in B: no input is left unmapped and none is mapped twice. Geometrically the rule becomes the vertical line test — a curve is the graph of a function exactly when every vertical line meets it at most once. Classification then splits two ways. Injective, or one-one, means distinct inputs keep distinct images; surjective, or onto, means every element of the codomain is hit; a function that is both is a bijection. Symmetry gives a second classification: f is even when f(−x) = f(x), giving a mirror about the y-axis, and odd when f(−x) = −f(x), giving a half-turn about the origin. Domain comes first in every case: a rule that divides by zero or takes a root of a negative is undefined there, and the domain must be stated before any other property.

items: Vertical line test: a graph represents a function only if no vertical line cuts it twice.
One-one: f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b; onto: every y in the codomain has some x with f(x) = y.
Even: f(−x) = f(x), symmetric about the y-axis; odd: f(−x) = −f(x), symmetric about the origin.
Find the domain first: denominators must be non-zero and radicands non-negative.
A many-one function such as f(x) = x² still qualifies as a function — the restriction is on inputs, not outputs.

items.text: The set {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)} is a function; {(1, 2), (1, 3)} is not
items.note: The element 1 carries two different images in the second set, breaking the one-image rule.

items.text: f(x) = 1/(x − 2) has domain all real numbers except x = 2, and f(x) = x² is even because (−x)² = x²
items.note: Exclude the zero of the denominator; verify evenness by substituting −x and simplifying.

keyPoints: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d; order is the content of a pair.
A × B holds n(A) × n(B) pairs and is not commutative unless A = B.
A relation is any subset of A × B; its domain and range are read from the pairs themselves.
The inverse relation reverses every pair, swapping the domain with the range.
Reflexive needs (a, a) everywhere, symmetric needs a return pair, transitive needs the closing pair.
An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive all at once.
A function gives every input exactly one image; the vertical line test is its graph form.
One-one means distinct inputs keep distinct images; onto means every codomain element is hit.
Even functions mirror about the y-axis; odd functions rotate by half a turn about the origin.
Find the domain before any classification: exclude zero denominators and negative radicands.
examFocus: State the three equivalence conditions in order and check them one at a time; each check carries its own mark.
When asked for domain and range, write them as sets — an interval or a listing, never the rule alone.
In one-one proofs, start from f(a) = f(b) and simplify to a = b; the implication direction is the mark.
Classify a function only after ruling on its domain, because a formula can be defined on a smaller set than it appears.

questions.prompt: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}, then n(A × B) is best computed as:
questions.explanation: The product rule gives n(A) × n(B) = 3 × 2 = 6 ordered pairs, since each of the three first components pairs with both second components.
All three self-pairs are present, every pair has its return, and every two-step path closes on an existing pair, so R satisfies all three conditions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following functions is odd?
questions.explanation: Substituting −x gives (−x)³ = −x³ = −f(x), which is exactly the odd condition; the other options fail it.

questions.prompt: The domain of the function f(x) = 1/(x − 2) is:
questions.explanation: The denominator vanishes at x = 2, so the rule is undefined there and the domain excludes that single value.

questions.prompt: The set of the first components of the ordered pairs of a relation is called its ______ .
questions.explanation: The domain collects the inputs; the second components instead form the range.

questions.prompt: A × B contains exactly ______ ordered pairs when A has 5 elements and B has 4.
questions.explanation: The product rule gives n(A) × n(B) = 5 × 4 = 20 pairs.

questions.prompt: State the three properties that a relation must satisfy to be an equivalence relation.
questions.answer: It must be reflexive — (a, a) belongs to R for every element a; symmetric — (a, b) in R implies (b, a) in R; and transitive — (a, b) and (b, c) in R imply (a, c) in R. All three must hold together, because an equivalence relation is exactly one that partitions its set into disjoint classes.
questions.explanation: The three conditions are independent, so each must be checked separately; equality of numbers is the standard example that satisfies all three.

questions.prompt: Define a function and state what makes a relation fail to be one.
questions.answer: A function is a relation in which every element of the domain has exactly one image in the codomain. A relation fails to be a function if some element of its domain has no image at all, or if any element carries two or more different images.
questions.explanation: One image per input is the whole rule; the mapping diagram shows the failure as two arrows leaving a single element.

questions.prompt: Let R = {(x, y) : x + y = 5, x, y ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4}}. Write R as a set of ordered pairs and state, with reasons, whether it is reflexive, symmetric or transitive on {1, 2, 3, 4}.
questions.answer: The pairs are R = {(1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1)}. It is symmetric, because (a, b) ∈ R always brings (b, a) ∈ R; it is not reflexive, since (1, 1) is missing; and it is not transitive, because (1, 4) and (4, 1) both lie in R while (1, 1) does not.
questions.explanation: List the pairs from the condition first, then test each property separately: one missing self-pair kills reflexivity, and a two-step path without its closing pair kills transitivity.

questions.prompt: Prove that the function f : ℝ → ℝ defined by f(x) = 2x + 3 is both one-one and onto, and hence state the value of f(4).
questions.answer: One-one: suppose f(a) = f(b); then 2a + 3 = 2b + 3, so 2a = 2b and a = b, which proves injectivity. Onto: for an arbitrary y ∈ ℝ choose x = (y − 3)/2, which is a real number, and f(x) = 2 · (y − 3)/2 + 3 = y, so every real number is an image. The function is therefore a bijection, and f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11.
questions.explanation: Both directions of the bijection must be shown: cancel to a = b for one-one, and construct the pre-image (y − 3)/2 for onto; the value of f(4) then follows by substitution.
